title: Ending the workday
hook: a clear end protects the rest of life

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus Aurelius, rising unwillingly to the work of a human being. Your line was begin with a breath.

The laptop is closed, but the work isn't. It comes along to dinner, rides home in a pocket, buzzes during a bedtime story, and lies awake in the dark. A workday with no ending doesn't stay where it was put. It leaks into everything else: the meal, the friend, the sleep. The opening pages of the Bible tell a story of work with its ending built in, and other traditions draw the line in their own ways. Today: Compline.
screen: `THE LAPTOP IS CLOSED.` → `THE WORK COMES HOME.` → `AN ENDING BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: First, Genesis. At the end of the sixth day, the King James Bible says, "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Then: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made." Look at it, call it good, end it. In this story the ending isn't an interruption of the making. It's part of it. Second, the Tao Te Ching. Its ninth chapter warns against filling a vessel to the brim and carrying it full, and against sharpening a blade so keen it can't keep its edge. When the work is done, it says, withdrawing is the way of Heaven. Not hanging on. Not one more email. Third, the monastery. The Rule of Benedict closes the monks' day with the night prayer called Compline, and after it, the Rule says, no one may speak. The day's work, and even the day's talk, gets a clear edge. Fourth, an ending for an ordinary job. It can be small. Look back at what got done, the way Genesis looks back, and let some of it be good. Write down what's left, so the mind can set it down. Then mark the line: a phrase, a closed door, a walk, a change of clothes. A clear end protects the rest of life: the people at home, the friends, the sleep. It also protects the work, which comes back the next morning to someone rested.
screen: `IT WAS VERY GOOD. GOD ENDED.` · `DON'T CARRY THE VESSEL FULL.` · `SILENCE AFTER COMPLINE.` · `LOOK BACK, WRITE IT DOWN, CLOSE.` · then, large: `DONE FOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing from today's work, or yesterday's, that got done, however small, and look at it for a moment, the way Genesis looks back. Then name one thing left undone, picture writing it down for tomorrow, and say silently: done for today. Let the shoulders drop; if you pray, you can close the work in your own tradition's words.
Compline. The monks' night prayer in the Rule of Benedict, after which no one may speak, giving the day a clear edge. Today's word.
Your line: done for today. In the story, the ending is part of the making. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns end the day with Compline and keep silence afterward; Jews and Christians read the close of the creation story in Genesis as a pattern of work that ends; readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its ninth chapter on stepping back when the work is done.

chat.says: Why end work on purpose? I'm just closing a laptop.
options: A clear ending keeps work from leaking into home and sleep; in Genesis, ending is part of making.
It doesn't really matter; work ends whenever you stop, and the mind lets go of it on its own.
Endings are for monks; in ordinary jobs, the more hours you stay on, the more gets done.
chat.meaning: In Genesis, God looks, calls it good, and ends. A clear end protects the people at home, the sleep, and the work itself.
